source.title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis : Finding Small , Trainable Neural Networks

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how initial network size and pruning relate to test accuracy and the training–test gap, using experiments different from the claim versions’ specified studies.
record.gate_note: The study does not train on random labels, compare convolutional with fully connected networks as a test of their generalization advantage, or measure optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example effects. Its pruning and reinitialization results are reported as tests of sparse trainability and initialization; only the explicitly reported network-size comparison and training–test accuracy results are included here. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out accuracy with and without dropout (V6) and reports Adam-versus-SGD comparisons (V4). Its sparse-subnetwork size comparison does not establish generalization beyond the width needed for zero training error (V2).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The central conclusion is that dense randomly initialized networks contain sparse subnetworks that can match the original network's test accuracy within comparable training iterations when reset to their original initializations. Selected tickets generalize better, and larger starting networks yield more accurate tickets at fixed remaining parameter counts. Random reinitialization generally degrades heavily pruned tickets; finding tickets in deeper networks depends on learning rate and warmup.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses iterative magnitude pruning and original-weight resetting, comparing sparse subnetworks and initial network sizes rather than directly testing the specified width sweep or other claim interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Initial network size changes validation accuracy at a fixed remaining parameter count; pruning level changes accuracy and early-stopping behavior. Learning rate and warmup affect whether the pruning procedure finds winning tickets in deeper networks.

fits_no_version.finding: At the same remaining parameter count, winning tickets from larger initial Lenet networks achieve higher validation accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger starting networks can yield more accurate sparse subnetworks through iterative magnitude pruning and original-weight resetting.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected winning tickets improve test accuracy while retaining approximately perfect training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Iterative magnitude pruning with original-weight resetting can reduce the training–test accuracy gap in the tested MNIST and CIFAR-10 classifiers.

record.problems: The experiments cover vision classification on MNIST and CIFAR-10, not larger datasets. Several comparisons are conveyed by figures; reported error bars give only trial minima and maxima. The width comparison uses validation accuracy of pruned subnetworks and does not isolate width beyond an interpolation threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows from the study’s pruning experiments were included where they measured learning speed, reinitialization performance, or test accuracy without a training–test gap comparison relevant to these versions. The study’s many hyperparameter and pruning-rate plots are not mapped to the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out accuracy compared with natural-label training.
Whether widening beyond the zero-training-error threshold continues lowering held-out error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Language benchmarks, broader optimizer tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching optimizers, and comparisons at matched training performance.
Batch-size interventions under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Very small training sets, excessive dropout, fully connected dropout experiments, and removing dropout together with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness of trained networks and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing memorized training examples versus randomly selected examples.

missing.what: Add dropout-versus-no-dropout rows for unpruned Conv-2, Conv-4, and Conv-6: mean test accuracy improves by 2.1, 3.0, and 2.4 percentage points. Dropout rate is 0.5; learning rates are selected separately and training budgets are tripled to 60K, 75K, and 90K iterations. These recipe differences must accompany the comparisons.
missing.locator: Section 3, Dropout; Figure 6; Appendices H.1 and H.5

missing.what: Add the explicit cross-optimizer result for unpruned CIFAR-10 Conv-2/4/6: despite learning-rate searches, SGD typically achieves validation accuracy 2–3 percentage points below Adam. Higher SGD rates cause exploding gradients and lower rates can fail to learn. Record the stated comparison rather than treating individual tuning candidates as independent findings.

Add the stated comparison on pruned MNIST Lenet networks: SGD rates 0.4 and 0.8 achieve validation accuracy equivalent to the best Adam rates, 0.0012 and 0.002. The reported advantage in maintaining early-stopping speed at greater sparsity is a separate measure.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V4 or V6. The V2 limits_scope label confuses an untested requirement with evidence limiting the claim. Dropout comparisons support the adapted recipe tested here; they do not isolate dropout at identical learning rates and training budgets. Optimizer comparisons establish held-out performance differences without establishing equal training performance.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization in the same recipes.
One-hidden-layer ReLU networks; downsampled CIFAR-10; a direct width sweep around the zero-training-error threshold.
A controlled comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks’ test error.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum on held-out performance.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets.
A dropout intervention’s effect on test error across training-set sizes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.operation_detail: Compared iterative-pruning results across initial network sizes, including test accuracy at the same remaining parameter count.
rows.measure: Validation accuracy at early stopping, compared across initial sizes at the same number of remaining weights.
rows.value: For any particular number of weights, winning tickets from initially larger networks reach higher accuracy.
rows.locator: Appendix G.6, Figure 31 and accompanying text
rows.note: This compares sparse subnetworks derived from different initial sizes; it does not directly measure test error across widths beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
rows.check: This measures validation accuracy of selected sparse subnetworks at equal remaining parameter counts. It does not establish zero training error or a width trend beyond interpolation. Remove its V2 link and associated limits_scope verdict.

rows.subject: Lenet-300-100

rows.measure: Training and test accuracy; the study reports training accuracy reaches 100% for nearly all networks and test accuracy improves by up to 0.35 percentage points.
rows.baseline: Original network at 50,000 iterations; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Test accuracy improves by up to 0.35 percentage points while training accuracy reaches 100% for nearly all networks.
rows.uncertainty: Average of five trials; error bars are minimum and maximum values.
rows.note: The authors infer a smaller training–test gap for winning tickets. The reported maximum improvement is not assigned to a specific pruning level in the text.
rows.check: The reported pruning improvement is supported, but it measures none of V1–V8. Its observed state describes pruning rather than a listed claim.
